**Stealth galaxies** are extreme [[low-luminosity-galaxies|Low-luminosity galaxies]] whose stellar densities fall at or below the background sky noise limit, rendering them virtually undetectable by traditional wide-field optical surveys. In the local Universe, these elusive objects represent the most diffuse, low-luminosity tail of [[dwarf-galaxy-populations|Dwarf Galaxy Populations]]. They are structurally characterized by extended half-light radii ($r_h > 100\text{ pc}$) and peak surface brightnesses typically fainter than $\mu \approx 30\text{ mag arcsec}^{-2}$ [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). Orbiting within the extended dark matter halos of massive hosts like the Milky Way, local stealth galaxies are theorized to be intrinsically metal-poor and gas-rich with small stellar [[galaxy-mass-to-light-ratio|Galaxy mass-to-light ratio]]s [McGaugh et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992PhDT.........7M/abstract), yet they possess exceptionally high dynamical mass-to-light ratios due to being overwhelmingly dark matter-dominated [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract). Because their detectability is severely hindered by surface brightness selection biases, their hypothesized existence plays a critical role in addressing the "missing satellite problem" and testing the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological framework on sub-galactic scales.

The evolutionary trajectory of local stealth galaxies is fundamentally governed by their physical environment, exhibiting a stark dichotomy between isolated and clustered systems. In the field, diffuse low-mass systems are overwhelmingly [[star-forming-galaxies|Star-forming galaxies]]; their shallow potential wells and dispersed star formation allow them to slowly and passively build their stellar mass over cosmic time [Geha et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...757...85G/abstract). Conversely, stealth systems that exist as [[satellite-galaxies|Satellite galaxies]] and cross the virial radius of a massive host halo are subject to severe environmental quenching mechanisms, such as ram-pressure stripping and galaxy harassment. These interactions quickly strip their diffuse cold gas reservoirs, permanently transforming them into faint, [[quiescent-galaxies|Quiescent galaxies]] [Geha et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...757...85G/abstract). Across all environments, objects identified through [[low-surface-brightness-astronomy|Low Surface Brightness Astronomy]] are characterized by extended dark matter distributions and slowly rising rotation curves, indicative of remarkably low total matter surface densities. 

Beyond the [[local-volume-and-nearby-galaxy-studies|Local Volume and Nearby Galaxy Studies]], the "stealth" paradigm also encompasses a distinct population of massive, heavily dust-obscured galaxies in the [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|early Universe]] ($z > 3$). These high-redshift analogues are optically invisible to traditional surveys relying on [[lyman-break-selection-and-galaxies|Lyman-Break Selection and Galaxies]], yet they contribute massively to the cosmic star-formation rate density when observed at submillimeter and mid-infrared wavelengths . Recent discoveries of compact, highly obscured systems—such as [[little-red-dots-jwst|Little Red Dots (JWST)]]—have further complicated the census of early [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]]. This article outlines the physical properties and detection strategies for stealth galaxies across cosmic time, exploring their environmental quenching pathways, their internal kinematics, and the theoretical tensions they introduce. 

## Definition and Physical Characteristics

Physically, stealth galaxies are distinguished from known ultrafaint dwarfs primarily by their highly extended stellar distributions. While their total luminosities and stellar velocity dispersions are comparable to confirmed ultrafaint satellites, stealth galaxies are predicted to possess a half-light radius ($r_h$) exceeding $100\text{ pc}$ [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). Because their stellar mass is spread over a relatively large volume, their typical peak surface brightness is driven down to levels fainter than $\mu = 30\text{ mag arcsec}^{-2}$ [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract), rendering them nearly invisible to standard optical star-count surveys.

These systems are theorized to inhabit dark matter subhalos that are slightly less massive and less concentrated than those hosting higher surface brightness counterparts. Kinematic predictions suggest peak circular velocities of $V_c \sim 8\text{ km s}^{-1}$ and enclosed dynamical masses within $300\text{ pc}$ of roughly $5 \times 10^6 M_\odot$ [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). Like larger objects studied in [[low-surface-brightness-astronomy|Low Surface Brightness Astronomy]], stealth galaxies are expected to be extremely dark matter-dominated. This aligns with the broader observational trend that the dynamical [[galaxy-mass-to-light-ratio|Galaxy mass-to-light ratio]] ($M/L$) systematically increases with decreasing central surface brightness , [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract). While the stellar mass-to-light ratios of LSB spirals are generally comparable to their high-surface-brightness counterparts, they exhibit a significantly larger scatter [Sprayberry et al. (1994)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994PhDT........53S/abstract). Structurally, these quenched diffuse systems often overlap with [[spheroidal-galaxies|dwarf spheroidal (dSph)]] and dwarf elliptical (dE) classifications; however, dSphs can be physically distinguished by their notably shallower surface brightness gradients compared to dEs [Ann et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJS..217...27A/abstract). 

Despite their extreme diffuseness, observations of more massive LSB systems reveal that their [[optically-identified-star-clusters|globular cluster populations]] show no significant deviation from those found in normal spirals, suggesting they share similar early formation periods and stellar assembly conditions before expanding [Villegas et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008AJ....135..467V/abstract). Their rotation curves, where measurable, are predicted to rise slowly, indicative of low total matter surface densities . Compositionally, they are expected to be metal-poor and gas-rich, evolving at a significantly slower rate than high-surface-brightness systems [McGaugh et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992PhDT.........7M/abstract), [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract).

## Historical Development and the Missing Satellite Problem

The theoretical motivation for identifying stealth galaxies is deeply intertwined with the historical development of the missing satellite problem. In the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework, cosmological simulations predict that massive dark matter halos, such as that of the Milky Way, should be populated by thousands of self-bound dark matter subhalos. However, the observed number of [[galactic-satellite-galaxies|Galactic satellite galaxies]] historically fell short of these theoretical predictions by several orders of magnitude. 

To resolve this discrepancy, two primary theoretical pathways were established. The first posits a strict low-mass threshold for galaxy formation, driven by early-universe reionization and internal stellar feedback, which renders the vast majority of low-mass subhalos entirely dark. The second suggests that the discrepancy is substantially exacerbated by severe observational selection biases against extended, diffuse stellar systems. Historically, earlier work also suggested that the excess population of faint blue galaxies observed at intermediate redshifts could act as high-redshift analogues to local low-surface-brightness systems, further emphasizing the role of diffuse populations in cosmological balances [McGaugh et al. (1994)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994Natur.367..538M/abstract). Furthermore, early spectroscopic surveys of faint red galaxies frequently uncovered [[low-redshift-star-forming-galaxies|Low-redshift star-forming galaxies]], even when the samples were initially selected based on their presumptively old stellar content, highlighting the severe challenges of purely photometric LSB characterization [Tresse et al. (1993)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1993A&A...277...53T/abstract). To fully understand these cosmic balances, one must also account for the broader evolution of the galaxy population: for example, the mass density of [[high-mass-quiescent-galaxies|High-mass quiescent galaxies]] has undergone a factor-of-10 increase from $z \sim 2$ to the present day, primarily driven by the ongoing transformation and quenching of the star-forming population [Brammer et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...739...24B/abstract).

Building upon the latter interpretation of selection biases, Bullock et al. proposed the specific existence of "stealth galaxies"—a hidden population of low-luminosity dwarf galaxies orbiting within the Milky Way halo [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). The existence of stealth galaxies introduces significant tension regarding the "common mass scale" frequently inferred for Milky Way satellites. Observations of known ultrafaint dwarfs suggest a preferred dynamical mass scale, but the literature conflicts on whether this is a genuine physical threshold for galaxy formation or merely an artifact of selection bias against low stellar density objects [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). If no strict low-mass threshold exists for baryon retention and star formation, extended stealth galaxies could number in the hundreds within the Milky Way halo alone, acting as a major component of the [[unseen-satellite-galaxies|Unseen satellite galaxies]] population. Conversely, if a physical truncation in galaxy formation efficiency strictly occurs at low halo masses—which would explain the surprisingly high densities of the confirmed ultrafaint dwarfs—then stealth galaxies may be exceedingly rare, numbering only in the single digits locally [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). 

Obtaining a complete census of these unseen systems provides a critical test of the $\Lambda$CDM framework on sub-galactic scales. Confirming or refuting the stealth galaxy paradigm ultimately demands advanced observational infrastructure, relying on deeper [[cosmic-surveys|Cosmic surveys]] and future 30-40m class telescopes equipped to perform spatially resolved spectroscopy on ultra-low-mass targets [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract), [Aguerri et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251214783A/abstract).

## Detection Strategies and Observational Techniques

The primary observational hurdle in identifying stealth galaxies is their extreme diffuseness. Because their surface densities fall well below the surface brightness of the night sky, they routinely escape detection in conventional broad-band imaging campaigns. Assessing their true abundance requires specialized detection strategies to separate genuine, self-bound stellar groupings from background fluctuations and foreground galactic cirrus.

In the immediate Local Volume (within roughly $5\text{ Mpc}$), all-sky [[extragalactic-astronomical-surveys|Extragalactic astronomical surveys]] have historically succeeded in doubling the known census of nearby dwarf galaxies, with subsequent follow-up programs employing Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB) distances to precisely determine their physical properties [Grebel et al. (2000)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2000ASPC..221..147G/abstract). Building on such foundational work, modern resources like the 50 Mpc Galaxy Catalog (50 MGC) have recently introduced homogenized mass, distance, color, and morphological data for over 15,000 nearby galaxies, providing an essential foundation for identifying extreme low-surface-brightness outliers in the local Universe [Ohlson et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024AJ....167...31O/abstract). Recent advancements in deep imaging with wide-field cameras have further expanded the search volume for faint [[satellite-galaxies|Satellite galaxies]]. Instruments such as the Subaru [[hyper-suprime-cam-surveys|Hyper Suprime-Cam Surveys]] have been instrumental in surveying the environments around nearby massive hosts, identifying dozens of new dwarf galaxy candidates around isolated spirals like M106 and NGC 3521. Artificial galaxy injection experiments demonstrate that these observations maintain completeness down to mean effective surface brightnesses of $\approx 26\text{ mag arcsec}^{-2}$ [Müller et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250411608M/abstract). Interestingly, even modest-aperture facilities utilizing very long exposure times, such as the Dwarf Galaxy Survey with Amateur Telescopes, have successfully identified extended low-surface-brightness features with effective surface brightnesses between $25.3$ and $28.8\text{ mag arcsec}^{-2}$ [Javanmardi et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016A&A...588A..89J/abstract). Because visual classification of diffuse, highly disturbed morphologies is complex, citizen science initiatives like Galaxy Zoo have dramatically improved the efficiency of identifying rare ram-pressure stripping features in such transforming galaxies [Crossett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025A&A...694A.204C/abstract).

Multiwavelength approaches and cosmic surveys are also essential in constructing a complete census. Combining optical data with high-sensitivity near-infrared imaging helps constrain the spectral energy distributions of faint targets. The 2MASS Large Galaxy Atlas has notably served as a foundational all-sky near-infrared census, providing a dust-penetrated view of galaxy morphologies uniquely sensitive to the dominant mass components of galaxies [Jarrett et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2003AJ....125..525J/abstract). Furthermore, cross-matching optical surveys with near-infrared imaging from missions like 2MASS and ultraviolet data from [[galex|GALEX]] allows astronomers to estimate stellar masses, ages, and star formation histories for [[low-mass-galaxies|Low-mass galaxies]] [Sánchez-Janssen et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011IAUS..277..230S/abstract).

For stealth systems within the Milky Way halo and the Local Group, discovery heavily relies on the analysis of resolved stellar populations. Deep photometric surveys identify stealth galaxies as localized statistical overdensities of resolved stars, often requiring extensive follow-up to confirm their gravitationally bound nature. However, establishing the internal kinematics, chemical enrichment, and dark matter halo properties of these ultra-low-mass systems ($M_* \sim 10^5 - 10^7 M_{\odot}$) remains a profound challenge for [[local-volume-and-nearby-galaxy-studies|Local Volume and Nearby Galaxy Studies]]. Current spectroscopic limits underscore the need for future 30-40m class telescopes equipped with multiplexed optical integral-field spectrographs to achieve a complete spectroscopic census [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract), [Aguerri et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251214783A/abstract). Modern spectroscopic efforts, such as the Dwarf Galaxy Integral-field Survey (DGIS), are already paving the way by providing a comprehensive, spatially resolved census of galaxies with stellar masses below $10^9 M_\odot$, crucial for mapping these faint kinematic structures [Li et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250104943L/abstract).

Finally, novel multi-messenger techniques have been proposed to overcome observational biases, particularly the obscuration caused by the Galactic disk. It has been suggested that future space-based gravitational wave observatories, such as LISA, could detect unseen satellite galaxies by observing the continuous gravitational wave emission from their constituent short-period double white dwarf binaries. This method would be entirely unaffected by dust extinction, potentially revealing a hidden population of stealth galaxies currently obscured by the Milky Way's midplane [Roebber et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...894L..15R/abstract).

## Environmental Context and Quenching Mechanisms

The evolutionary trajectory of stealth galaxies and related low surface brightness (LSB) systems is fundamentally governed by their local environment. Observational surveys demonstrate that the cessation of star formation in these [[low-mass-galaxies|Low-mass galaxies]] is almost entirely an environmental process driven primarily by their host halo mass, as isolated dwarfs are rarely quenched [Haines et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007ASPC..379..206H/abstract).

In isolated environments, low-mass galaxies are overwhelmingly active. For field dwarf galaxies with stellar masses below a strict threshold of $M_* < 1.0 \times 10^9 M_\odot$, the fraction of quenched systems is observationally constrained to an upper limit of less than $0.06\%$ [Geha et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...757...85G/abstract). Consequently, nearly 100% of these isolated systems show evidence of recent star formation. Demographic studies confirm that isolated environments are overwhelmingly dominated by [[late-type-galaxies-and-stellar-populations|Late-type Galaxies and Stellar Populations]] (constituting approximately $77.6\%$ of the population); furthermore, the rare isolated early-type galaxies that do exist are typically $50\%$ less massive than their cluster-dwelling counterparts [Khim et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJS..220....3K/abstract). Structurally extended stealth galaxies tend to favor low-density regions of the cosmic web, such as filaments and voids, actively avoiding the central regions of rich clusters [Rosenbaum et al. (2004)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004A&A...422L...5R/abstract), [Pérez-Montaño et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.490.3772P/abstract). Specialized morphological classes sharing LSB traits, such as "Little Blue Spheroids," are found in extreme isolation in roughly $65\%$ of cases, which preserves their star-forming state [Moffett et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.489.2830M/abstract). In the most extreme low-density environments, such as cosmic voids, LSB systems tend to be predominantly blue, disk-like, and feature notably higher specific star formation rates than equivalents found in denser environments [Hoyle et al. (2005)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2005AAS...206.1002H/abstract). Furthermore, these cosmic voids exhibit a significant deficit of luminous and normal red galaxies compared to denser wall regions, suggesting that environment-dependent merger histories strongly influence the overall red galaxy population [Bruton et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.491.2496B/abstract).

Conversely, the population of quenched, [[passive-galaxies|Passive galaxies]]—often classified morphologically as dwarf spheroidals (dSph) or dwarf ellipticals (dE)—is found almost exclusively in the guise of [[satellite-galaxies|Satellite galaxies]] bound to massive host halos. The vast majority of these quiescent dwarfs reside strictly within two virial radii (typically $\sim 1.5 \text{ Mpc}$) of massive [[central-galaxies|Central galaxies]] [Geha et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...757...85G/abstract). This environmental quenching of satellites contrasts sharply with the formation of isolated early-type galaxies, which may instead assemble passively through major mergers or the collapse of small, isolated groups rather than ram-pressure or harassment [Reda et al. (2004)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004MNRAS.354..851R/abstract). 

The transition from blue, [[star-forming-galaxies|Star-forming galaxies]] to red, quiescent satellites is driven by a suite of environmental quenching mechanisms. As a stealth galaxy falls into the dense intracluster or intragroup medium of a massive host, it experiences significant hydrodynamical and gravitational forces. In massive structures such as the A2142 cluster, star formation activity is observed to be inhibited progressively from the cluster outskirts to the center, with transitioning galaxies often found favoring localized substructures [Qu et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023RAA....23h5007Q/abstract). The primary mechanisms responsible for shutting down star formation include ram-pressure stripping, which rapidly removes the galaxy's cold interstellar gas reservoir, and "suffocation" (or strangulation), which strips the extended hot gas halo and prevents further cosmological gas accretion [Haines et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007ASPC..379..206H/abstract). Additionally, frequent high-speed encounters within the cluster potential (galaxy harassment) can dynamically heat the stellar component, fundamentally altering the dwarf's morphology while accelerating gas loss. Adding complexity to these morphological transitions is the existence of "Red Misfits"—a subpopulation comprising approximately $11\%$ of galaxies that exhibit red colors but remain actively star-forming, likely representing a transitional stage driven by internal quenching processes rather than global environmental effects [Evans et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.476.5284E/abstract). Interestingly, while massive cluster-scale environmental processes dominate many dwarf transformations, observations of post-starburst (E+A) galaxies suggest that rapid quenching can also be driven by localized dynamical interactions at scales below $100\text{ kpc}$ rather than global cluster-scale effects [Goto et al. (2005)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2005MNRAS.357..937G/abstract). These post-starburst systems additionally exhibit a cosmic downsizing trend over time, where their peak absolute magnitudes shift progressively fainter, from $M \sim -23.5$ at $z \sim 0.8$ to $M \sim -20.3$ at $z \sim 0.1$ [Pattarakijwanich et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...833...19P/abstract).

Because stealth galaxies are heavily dark matter-dominated and possess characteristically low baryonic surface densities [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract), their diffuse gas reservoirs are particularly susceptible to these stripping processes. Consequently, while stealth galaxies in the field evolve slowly over cosmic time, those that cross the virial radius of a massive neighbor face a rapid truncation of their star formation histories, transitioning permanently into the quiescent dwarf galaxy populations observed in the Local Group and nearby clusters.

## Formation Scenarios and Evolutionary Pathways

The evolutionary history of stealth galaxies is generally divided into two primary theoretical frameworks: in situ primordial formation and secondary environmental generation. 

In the context of cosmological hierarchical assembly, stealth galaxies may arise naturally from modest initial density fluctuations in the early Universe [McGaugh et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992PhDT.........7M/abstract). These primordial systems are predicted to inhabit dark matter subhalos that are slightly less massive, yet significantly more extended, than those hosting typical high-surface-brightness ultrafaint dwarfs [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). If hierarchical assembly proceeds without a sharp low-mass cutoff for baryon retention, such stealth galaxies born from initial low-density fluctuations could be ubiquitous, numbering in the hundreds around massive halos and constituting a substantial fraction of the unseen [[satellite-galaxies|Satellite galaxies]] [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract).

Alternatively, stealth systems may form dynamically as tidal dwarf galaxies generated during violent galaxy interactions and mergers. In dense group and cluster environments, tidal forces can liberate gas and stellar material from massive parent galaxies, which may subsequently self-gravitate to form low-density dwarfs [Okazaki et al. (2000)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2000ApJ...543..149O/abstract). The literature remains divided on the exact evolutionary mapping of these objects; while some studies treat extreme low-surface-brightness galaxies strictly as a distinct primordial population, others argue they may be "disappearing dwarfs"—formerly normal galaxies that have faded and expanded following severe environmental mass loss and gas stripping [Phillipps et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995MNRAS.274..832P/abstract). Interestingly, deep optical imaging reveals that star-forming blue early-type galaxies often display extended, low-surface-brightness features indicative of recent mergers; these systems are thought to represent a critical transition stage before fully settling into [[passive-galaxies|passive]], early-type morphologies [George et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...678A..10G/abstract).

Regardless of their precise formation channel, the subsequent evolution of stealth galaxies remains heavily dictated by their environment, reflecting the stark field/satellite dichotomy [Geha et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...757...85G/abstract). Isolated systems are expected to remain gas-rich and metal-poor, evolving at a significantly slower rate than their high-surface-brightness counterparts and potentially forming stars outside of standard giant molecular cloud environments [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract). Conversely, those operating as satellites within massive halos undergo dense-environment interactions that rapidly strip their remaining cold gas, terminating star formation and transforming them into faint, quiescent galaxies populated entirely by old stellar populations [Haines et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007ASPC..379..206H/abstract).

## High-Redshift Analogues and Optically Invisible Populations

While the local Universe defines "stealth" galaxies by their diffuse structures and extreme low surface brightnesses, the concept of a stealth population extends into the early Universe in the form of massive, highly obscured galaxies. At redshifts $z > 3$, rest-frame ultraviolet surveys—such as those employing [[lyman-break-selection-and-galaxies|Lyman-Break Selection and Galaxies]]—routinely miss a substantial fraction of [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] due to severe dust attenuation. Historically, this stealth phenomenon was recognized through [[extremely-red-objects|Extremely Red Objects (EROs)]] at $z \approx 1\text{--}2$, which are understood to be a mix of passively evolving older systems and heavily dust-obscured starbursts that act as the high-mass progenitors of local elliptical galaxies [McCarthy et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004ARA&A..42..477M/abstract). This reflects a broader pattern of [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|galaxy mass downsizing]] observed at high redshifts ($z \sim 1\text{--}3.5$), where the most massive galaxies are already in place early on, while the low-mass population evolves significantly later, contributing to steep stellar mass functions at these epochs [Mortlock et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.413.2845M/abstract).

Submillimetre observations at $870 \, \mu\mathrm{m}$ have revealed a dominant population of optically invisible massive galaxies at $z > 3$ . These sub-millimeter galaxies represent the high-mass, dusty tail of the star-forming population, providing extreme benchmarks that challenge current hierarchical formation models [Cirasuolo et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008ASPC..399..153C/abstract). Despite remaining undetected in deep optical and near-infrared bands, these systems exhibit [[vigorous-star-formation|Vigorous star formation]] with typical rates of $\mathrm{SFR} \approx 200 \, M_\odot \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. With an estimated comoving space density of $2 \times 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, this stealth population contributes a cosmic star-formation rate density approximately a factor of ten higher than that of equivalently massive UV-bright galaxies at the same epoch. They are consequently considered the likely progenitors of the most massive present-day galaxies residing in dense clusters . This evolutionary link is further supported by observations showing that massive galaxies at $1.4 < z < 2.5$ exhibit strong clustering and are predominantly [[star-forming-galaxies|Star-forming galaxies]], effectively acting as the direct progenitors for present-day massive galaxy clusters [Furusawa et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...727..111F/abstract). Furthermore, multi-wavelength studies of submillimeter-selected galaxies indicate that their molecular gas fraction steadily declines with increasing stellar mass, suggesting a clear evolutionary trend as these obscured starbursts consume their gas reservoirs [Hainline et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008PhDT.......251H/abstract). A persistent question in this field is whether these high-redshift submillimeter-selected objects represent a fundamentally distinct galaxy population or simply extreme members of the general star-forming population undergoing intense, short-lived starburst phases [Dunlop et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011arXiv1108.5679D/abstract). Because spectroscopic confirmation of these optically dark targets is notoriously difficult, astronomers have successfully employed neighbor-clustering analyses to statistically verify the high-redshift identity and immense dark matter halo masses of these candidate massive galaxies prior to obtaining deep spectra [Muñoz et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008MNRAS.385.2175M/abstract). Observations of massive galaxies at $z \sim 4$ further reveal that they exhibit preferentially lower specific star formation rates in their centers compared to their outer regions, providing strong evidence for inside-out quenching within these early massive systems [Jung et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...834...81J/abstract).

The phenomenon of optically thick dust obscuration also creates stealth components within otherwise normal, UV-bright star-forming galaxies. Spatially resolved spectral energy distribution modeling of galaxies with $\log(M_*/M_\odot) > 10.3$ at $2.5 < z < 3.5$ indicates that approximately $33\%$ contain localized, optically thick dust substructures. These obscured regions can hide $10\%$ to $20\%$ of a galaxy's total stellar mass and star formation rate [Cheng et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...979...71C/abstract). Furthermore, mid-infrared observations reveal that the underlying rest-frame near-infrared morphologies of these galaxies are often smooth and disk-like, tracing mature stellar populations that contrast sharply with their irregular and clumpy UV appearances [Costantin et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240700153C/abstract).

Pushing the boundaries of the stealth paradigm, recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have uncovered a population of compact, highly obscured systems at $z \gtrsim 7$, colloquially known as [[little-red-dots-jwst|Little Red Dots (JWST)]]. These targets include intrinsically red candidate galaxies with stellar masses exceeding $10^{10} \, M_\odot$ located $500\text{--}700$ Myr after the Big Bang ($7.4 \leq z \leq 9.1$) [Labbé et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023Natur.616..266L/abstract). Distinct from these heavily obscured red sources, JWST has also confirmed extremely luminous, yet exceptionally blue systems ($M_{\mathrm{uv}} = -20.81 \pm 0.16$, featuring steep ultraviolet slopes and no detected emission lines) out to $z \approx 14.3$, representing a fundamentally different population of early, stellar-continuum-dominated galaxies [Carniani et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240518485C/abstract). 

The physical nature of Little Red Dots remains a subject of active debate in the literature. Their broad emission lines and compact sizes suggest they may be powered by central overmassive black holes and could represent a low-spin tail of the galaxy population undergoing highly efficient, centrally concentrated star formation [Loeb et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024RNAAS...8..182L/abstract). Regardless of their precise powering mechanisms, the unexpectedly high abundance and rapid assembly of these massive, optically faint systems in the early Universe is currently in tension with standard hierarchical models of [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|High-Redshift Galaxy Evolution]] [Labbé et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023Natur.616..266L/abstract).

## Kinematics and Dark Matter Distribution

The internal kinematics of stealth galaxies and the broader population of [[low-surface-brightness-astronomy|low surface brightness (LSB) systems]] are defined by extreme dark matter domination. As previously noted, mass modeling of local stealth satellites indicates they inhabit low-mass subhalos ($V_c \sim 8\text{ km s}^{-1}$), resulting in highly extended, low-density dark matter distributions that are substantially less concentrated than the halos surrounding high surface brightness (HSB) spirals [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract), [de Blok et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997ASPC..117...39D/abstract). For massive hosts orbited by stealth satellites, the central stellar velocity dispersion of the [[central-galaxies|primary galaxy]] has been shown to act as a robust tracer of its total underlying dark matter halo mass, aiding in the dynamical mapping of the host-satellite system [Seo et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...903..130S/abstract).

The distribution of mass within these systems is most clearly traced by their rotation curves and gas profiles. The rotation curves of LSB galaxies rise much more slowly than those of HSB galaxies of equivalent total luminosity, typically reaching maximum velocity amplitudes between $50$ and $120\text{ km s}^{-1}$ . In many cases, these rotation curves are still rising at the outermost measured radii, underscoring the extended nature of their gravitational potentials and indicating exceptionally low matter surface densities . The gaseous components of these galaxies follow a similarly diffuse profile. The HI surface density in LSB systems is typically a factor of $\sim 3$ lower than in normal late-type galaxies . In denser environments, global [[h-i-rich-galaxies|H I-deficiency]] maps and new scaling relations are frequently used to identify clusters where environmental factors have systematically stripped the neutral gas from cluster galaxies, a process that severely impacts the extended disks of LSB systems [Dénes et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014MNRAS.444..667D/abstract). Despite this diffuse gas distribution, undisturbed LSB galaxies often remain highly gas-rich, featuring extended neutral hydrogen disks that act as excellent kinematic tracers for the underlying dark matter halos well beyond the optical extent of the galaxy [Chengalur et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008ASSP....5...65C/abstract).

The combination of low stellar density and massive, extended dark matter halos results in a highly elevated [[galaxy-mass-to-light-ratio|Galaxy mass-to-light ratio]]. Observations confirm that both the dynamical mass-to-light ratio ($M_{\rm dyn}/L$) and the neutral gas mass-to-light ratio ($M_{\rm HI}/L$) systematically increase as the central surface brightness of the galaxy decreases , [Bothun et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997PASP..109..745B/abstract). In terms of broader mass assembly and the relation between stellar and dark matter content, observations reveal that at $z = 1$, satellite galaxies dominate the red sequence below the knee of the mass function, while the subsequent growth of the red sequence toward the present day is driven primarily by the ongoing quenching of low-mass central galaxies [Tinker et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...778...93T/abstract).

Furthermore, the structural diffuseness of stealth and LSB galaxies is strongly linked to their angular momentum. Kinematic studies demonstrate that LSB galaxies possess systematically higher values of the dimensionless spin parameter, $\lambda$, than their HSB counterparts. Direct measurements utilizing spatially resolved kinematics confirm that the spin parameter of LSB galaxies is typically $1.6$ to $2$ times larger than that of comparable HSB galaxies [Pérez-Montaño et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.490.3772P/abstract). While the magnitude of a galaxy's spin strongly influences its structural diffuseness, the purely geometric direction of rotation does not seem to intrinsically alter its physical properties; large-scale surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) have shown no significant photometric difference based on the spin direction (clockwise versus counterclockwise) of spiral galaxies [Hoehn et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014AN....335..189H/abstract). This elevated spin parameter naturally leads to more extended centrifugal support, preventing the gas from collapsing into high-density regions. Consequently, star formation thresholds are rarely met, helping to explain why stealth and LSB galaxies evolve at a significantly slower rate and remain in an early, unevolved state compared to conventional members of the Hubble sequence , [de Blok et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997ASPC..117...39D/abstract).

## Open Questions and Future Directions

A central unresolved issue in local [[extragalactic-astronomy|Extragalactic astronomy]] remains whether the "common mass scale" observed among Milky Way [[satellite-galaxies|Satellite galaxies]] represents a genuine physical threshold for galaxy formation or merely an artifact of surface brightness selection bias [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). If no low-mass threshold exists, theories predict that hundreds of elusive stealth galaxies may reside undetected in the Local Group. Conversely, if the density of ultrafaint dwarfs reflects a strict mass cutoff in galaxy formation, the Milky Way halo may host only a handful of such systems.

Overcoming current photometric completeness limits is a primary driver for next-generation instrumentation. Establishing a true census of stealth and [[low-luminosity-galaxies|Low-luminosity galaxies]] will require 30m-class observatories [Bullock et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717.1043B/abstract). Future extremely large telescopes (ELT/TMT), particularly those equipped with multiplexed optical integral-field spectrographs, will extend spatially resolved spectroscopy to ultra-low-mass dwarfs ($M_* \sim 10^5 - 10^7 M_\odot$) far beyond the Local Group. This will enable astronomers to map internal kinematics, chemical enrichment, and star-formation histories across diverse environments out to the Coma Cluster [Aguerri et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251214783A/abstract). In parallel, non-electromagnetic detection methods, such as utilizing the LISA gravitational wave observatory to detect white dwarf binaries, are highly anticipated to bypass traditional completeness limits and unveil stealth systems completely obscured by the Galactic disk [Roebber et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...894L..15R/abstract).

Finally, the concept of stealth galaxies extends to [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|High-Redshift Galaxy Evolution]], where the observational challenge shifts to massive, optically dark systems. A major open question is whether the abundance of massive, dust-obscured galaxies at $z > 3$—and extending to $z > 10$—can be reconciled with standard $\Lambda$CDM models of hierarchical galaxy assembly. Recent early-release observations from JWST have spectroscopically confirmed unexpectedly luminous and massive galaxies ($M_* \sim 10^{10} - 10^{11} M_\odot$) already in place merely 300-700 Myr after the Big Bang [Labbé et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023Natur.616..266L/abstract), alongside exceptionally bright blue systems extending out to $z \approx 14.3$ [Carniani et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240518485C/abstract). 

The literature is currently in active debate over these optically faint [[little-red-dots-jwst|Little Red Dots (JWST)]]. While some authors interpret them as a dominant, previously unseen population of massive galaxies that contribute heavily to the early cosmic star-formation-rate density , others argue this tension may be resolved if these objects represent a low-spin tail of the galaxy population hosting over-massive central black holes, or systems with optically thick dust substructures that artificially inflate inferred stellar masses [Loeb et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024RNAAS...8..182L/abstract), [Cheng et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241108100C/abstract). Resolving whether these primordial stealth galaxies violate current cosmological paradigms will be a central goal of future [[deep-field-campaigns|Deep field campaigns]].
